summary: Corrects and clarifies RFC 3095, which defines RObust Header Compression and profiles for IP, UDP, RTP and ESP. Parts of the original were unclear or mistaken in ways that could cause interoperability problems.

eli5.summary: Packet headers are like repeated address labels. ROHC shrinks them. This fixes mistakes in the original instructions so different makers' products work together.

questions: what does rfc 4815 correct in rfc 3095
how is the rohc crc calculated
subtitle: A list of fixes and clarifications that let different ROHC implementations of RFC 3095 actually interoperate.

tldr.problem: Interoperability testing of RFC 3095 (RObust Header Compression) found ambiguous text, common misreadings and a few outright errors that could stop different implementations from working together.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4815 quotes the faulty RFC 3095 text, labels it INCOMPLETE, INCORRECT or INCORRECT AND INVALIDATED, and gives CORRECTED text or a FORMAL ADDITION. It covers CRC coverage, mode transitions, timestamp encoding, list compression, context updates and context reuse.
tldr.outcome: References to RFC 3095 should now also include this document. It also updates RFC 3241, RFC 3843, RFC 4019 and RFC 4362, and it changes nothing about security.

today: RFC 4815 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it. It updates RFC 3095, RFC 3241, RFC 3843, RFC 4019 and RFC 4362, so implementers of those documents should read it alongside them.

sections.title: Why a Corrections Document
sections.content:
RFC 3095 defines the RObust Header Compression (ROHC) framework and profiles for IP, UDP, RTP and ESP. During implementation and interoperability testing, people found ambiguities, common misinterpretations and a few errors. RFC 4815 collects them and gives the fixes needed for implementations to interoperate, so it is an update to RFC 3095. References to RFC 3095 should also include this document.

It also corrects or clarifies RFC 3241 (ROHC over PPP), RFC 3843 (the ROHC IP-only profile) and RFC 4019 (the ROHC UDP-Lite profiles). RFC 4362 is implicitly updated because it is also based on RFC 3095.

Where it changes the old text, it quotes the original and labels it INCOMPLETE, INCORRECT or INCORRECT AND INVALIDATED, followed by CORRECTED text. New rules that fix no existing sentence are labeled FORMAL ADDITION.
sections.eli5: A rulebook had some confusing pages. This document lists each confusing page, shows what it said, and then says what it should have said.

sections.title: CRC Calculation and Coverage
sections.content:
RFC 3095 gives polynomials for 3-, 7- and 8-bit CRCs but never names the algorithm. RFC 4815 says all three use the CRC algorithm defined in RFC 1662, and Appendix A supplies a sample implementation in Perl.

Three coverage details are fixed. The CRC in IR and IR-DYN packets now excludes the payload and the padding, and it does not cover the Add-CID octet for CID 0. The 8-bit CRC in the feedback CRC option covers the feedback payload including any CID fields, but excludes the packet type, the Size field and the Code octet. For the ESP NULL header, the CRC covers only the initial part (the SPI and sequence number), not the trailer after the payload.
sections.eli5: A CRC is a secret handshake number that proves a message was not scrambled. Both sides must agree on exactly which parts of the message go into the number, and this section says which.

sections.title: Mode Transitions
sections.content:
In RFC 3095 the decompressor had to send feedback for every packet while its D_TRANS parameter was I (Initiated). RFC 4815 lets a decompressor optionally use a Pending state, P, in the second half of a transition to Optimistic or Unidirectional mode. While D_TRANS is P, feedback need not accompany each packet, but the decompressor MUST keep sending feedback with some periodicity and every such packet MUST carry the CRC option. Without that rule, lost feedback could leave a transition from R-mode deadlocked. The change does not affect interoperability with an RFC 3095 compressor.

The compressor MUST ignore mode-transition feedback that is not protected by the CRC option. In R-mode, an acknowledgement sent while D_TRANS is I MUST use the sequence number of the packet that last updated the context, not that of an R-0 or R-1* packet. Packets of type 0 or 1 received before the decompressor acknowledges the new mode are decoded with the old mode, and afterwards with the new one.
sections.eli5: Switching how two walkie-talkie users talk takes a three-step handshake. The new rule lets one side stop saying okay after every sentence, as long as it still checks in now and then so nobody gets stuck waiting.

sections.title: RTP Timestamp Encoding
sections.content:
Timestamps (TS) are always W-LSB encoded, scaled or not. When a packet carries no TS bits, the decompressor extrapolates linearly from the sequence number: delta_TS = delta_SN * default-slope(TS). If such a packet arrives with Tsc = 0, the decompressor MUST discard it. The RFC 3095 sentence implying slopes other than the default is invalidated.

For scaled timestamps, TS = TS_SCALED * TS_STRIDE + TS_OFFSET. The old formula TS / TS_STRIDE is only valid if "/" is integer division and TS_STRIDE is greater than 0. The old approach of letting the decompressor cope with wraparound is declared neither interoperable nor robust. Instead, when TS_STRIDE is not a power of two, the compressor SHOULD reinitialize TS_OFFSET after a wraparound by sending an unscaled TS. The decompressor MUST recalculate TS_OFFSET whenever it receives an unscaled TS.

The interpretation interval is p = 2^(k-1) - 1 for timer-based compression (non-zero TIME_STRIDE) and p = 2^(k-2) - 1 otherwise. In Extension 3 the Tsc flag applies to all TS bits and scaling always uses context(TS_STRIDE). If TS_STRIDE is sent together with scaled TS, it MUST be ignored and discarded, so Tsc SHOULD NOT be set when Tss is set.
sections.eli5: Timestamps are like a clock that ticks the same amount for every packet. If the receiver knows the tick size, the sender only has to say which tick it is on, or nothing at all, and the receiver can work it out.

sections.title: List Compression and Updating Rules
sections.content:
Extension-header and CSRC lists are compressed with reference lists and index tables. Several points are settled. The Generic CSRC list in the RTP dynamic chain is always at least one octet, even when empty. The CC field appears twice in the dynamic part; the compressor MUST set both to the same value and the decompressor MUST use the one inside the Encoding Type 0 list. A 7-bit mask may be used for a longer list if only the first seven items change, and the decompressor MUST NOT touch items beyond the mask. Encoding types 1, 2 and 3 MUST refer to a non-empty reference list.

Each non-identical extension header of the same type MUST get its own index, and a compressor MUST NOT compress packets with more than one ESP NULL header unless the second-outermost header is treated as a regular ESP header under profile 0x0003. AH and GRE sequence numbers may be omitted only when their offset from the RTP sequence number is constant and the compressor is confident the decompressor knows it, replacing the earlier linear-increase wording.

On updating: UO-1-ID packets update only TS, SN, IP-ID and sequence numbers of IP extension headers, but the translation table MUST still be updated for every (Index, item) pair. An IR packet does not clear the whole context. The R-P bit and the X bit are set to zero in the context when their presence flags (R-PT, RX) are 0.
sections.eli5: When a list of items changes a little, the sender only says what was added or removed. This section makes sure both sides number and count the items the same way.

sections.title: Context Management and CID Reuse
sections.content:
Through the MAX_CID parameter, the decompressor agrees to host at least MAX_CID+1 contexts, and an established context within that space MUST be kept until the CID is reused or the channel is taken down or renegotiated. How CIDs are reused stays an implementation detail, but two cases need care.

With the same profile, the compressor SHOULD keep the old context's mode for the new context, because there is no reliable way to tell the decompressor that a reuse is happening and so no safe way to start a mode switch. With a different profile, both sides MUST start in the profile's initial mode. A CID whose context is in R-mode SHOULD NOT be reused for a different profile, since R-mode type 0 and type 1 packets have no CRC and can be misread if the initiating IR packets are lost.
sections.eli5: Contexts are like numbered coat-check tickets. When a ticket number is handed to a new coat, both sides must be sure the old coat is fully forgotten and nobody grabs the wrong one.

sections.title: Other Clarifications
sections.content:
Several smaller points are settled. The NBO bit means network byte order is used. IP-ID is the compressed Identification of the innermost IPv4 header whose RND flag is not 1; when RND or RND2 is 1 the value is sent as a 16-bit uncompressed field at the end of the compressed base header. If two Marker (M) bits appear in one compressed header, they must match or the packet MUST be discarded. Multiple SN options in one feedback packet are concatenated, which lets a 32-bit ESP sequence number be returned. Multiple CRC options are allowed only if all are identical; otherwise the compressor MUST discard the feedback packet.

If a feedback link is lost, the compressor SHOULD restart R-mode flows using a different CID for each. The optional ACK mechanism for UOR-2 in O-mode is NOT RECOMMENDED. When a compressor repairs a context after a NACK with UOR-2, it SHOULD include TS_STRIDE and TIME_STRIDE fields it has ever updated; after a static-NACK it MUST include them in the IR header.

On negotiation, a profile is a 16-bit value whose 8 least significant bits give the profile and 8 most significant bits the variant, so a negotiated PROFILES set MUST NOT include more than one variant of a profile. For ROHC over PPP, the same profile set MUST be negotiated for IPv4 (IPCP) and IPv6 (IPV6CP). The Constant IP-ID mechanism of RFC 3843 applies to both inner and outer IP headers, giving SID and SID2 context values.
sections.eli5: This is a list of small notes in the margin, such as which bit means what and what to do when a message is repeated or a phone line goes dead.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document corrects and clarifies RFC 3095 but makes no change to its security aspects. The security considerations of RFC 3095 therefore apply without additions.
sections.eli5: Nothing about safety changed, so the old safety rules still apply as they were.

items.label: Initiated
items.desc: Decompressor sends a NACK or ACK with a CRC option for each packet received.

items.label: Pending
items.desc: Feedback need not accompany every packet but must continue periodically, always with the CRC option.

items.label: Done
items.desc: Initial value; a mode transition can be initiated only when D_TRANS is D.
